questions.title: Two events that look dependent until the union is conditioned on
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 4.6 (use of Venn diagrams, tree diagrams, sample space diagrams and tables of outcomes; combined events, mutually exclusive events, conditional probability, independence)
questions.subtopic: 4.6 Venn diagrams, tree diagrams, sample space diagrams and tables of outcomes
questions.challenge_mechanism: Conditioning on the union rather than on a single event reverses the apparent dependence, so the independence test in part (c) does not settle part (d).
questions.question: Two events $H$ and $G$ in the same sample space satisfy $P(H)=0.6$, $P(G)=0.45$ and $P(H\cap G)=0.25$. Each part below refers to these two events.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find $P(H\cup G)$, the probability that at least one of the two events occurs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find $P(H\mid G)$ and $P(G\mid H)$, giving each answer as an exact fraction in its lowest terms.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine, showing your reasoning, whether the events $H$ and $G$ are independent.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Given that at least one of $H$ and $G$ occurs, find the probability that both occur.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The addition rule for two events gives $P(H\cup G)=P(H)+P(G)-P(H\cap G)$ **(M1)** $=0.6+0.45-0.25$ **(A1)** $=0.8$ **(A1)**, so the probability that at least one of the two events occurs is $0.8$ **(A1)**. The subtraction is needed because the outcomes lying in both events would otherwise be counted twice, so the rule is valid for any two events in the same sample space, whether or not those events are independent.

**(b)** The conditional probability formula gives $P(H\mid G)=\frac{P(H\cap G)}{P(G)}=\frac{0.25}{0.45}$ **(M1)** $=\frac{25}{45}=\frac{5}{9}$ **(A1)**. Applying the same formula the other way round, $P(G\mid H)=\frac{P(H\cap G)}{P(H)}=\frac{0.25}{0.6}$ **(M1)** $=\frac{25}{60}=\frac{5}{12}$ **(A1)**. Each conditional probability restricts attention to the conditioning event, so its denominator is the probability of that event alone, which is why the two fractions differ even though both use the same joint probability.

**(c)** Two events are independent precisely when $P(H\cap G)=P(H)P(G)$ **(M1)**. Here $P(H)P(G)=0.6\times 0.45=0.27$ **(A1)**, and this is not equal to the given value $0.25$ **(R1)**. Hence $H$ and $G$ are not independent **(A1)**, because the product of the separate probabilities fails to reproduce the joint probability.

**(d)** Conditioning on the union restricts the sample space to $H\cup G$ **(M1)**, so the required probability is $\frac{P(H\cap G)}{P(H\cup G)}$ **(A1)** $=\frac{0.25}{0.8}$ **(A1)** $=\frac{25}{80}=\frac{5}{16}=0.3125$ **(A1)**. This conditioning event is the union rather than a single event, so the quantity is different from either answer in part (b), and the calculation is correct because the definition of conditional probability applies to any event of positive probability.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for the addition rule with the intersection subtracted; the first (A1) is for substituting the three given probabilities, the second (A1) for the arithmetic, and the third (A1) for the final value $0.8$. A candidate who adds $0.6$ and $0.45$ and stops at $1.05$ earns only the (M1).

(b) Award (M1) for the conditional probability formula in each direction and (A1) for each exact fraction; decimals such as $0.5556$ do not earn the (A1). The two (M1) marks are independent, so a candidate who reverses the denominator for $P(G\mid H)$ still keeps the first pair.

(c) The (M1) is for stating the independence test, and the (A1) is for the product $0.27$. The (R1) requires an explicit comparison of $0.27$ with $0.25$, and the final (A1) is for the conclusion. A bare assertion of dependence without the product forfeits two marks.

(d) This is the discriminating part. The (M1) is for recognising that the conditioning event is the union, the (A1) for the quotient structure, the next (A1) for substituting $0.25$ and $0.8$, and the final (A1) for the exact value $\frac{5}{16}$ or its decimal $0.3125$. Follow through from an incorrect union is allowed provided the quotient is formed correctly.
questions.explanation:
The item turns on the difference between conditioning on one event and conditioning on the union of two events. Parts (a) to (c) establish the familiar facts: the union has probability $0.8$, the two conditional probabilities are $\frac{5}{9}$ and $\frac{5}{12}$, and the events are dependent because $0.6$ times $0.45$ is $0.27$ rather than $0.25$. A candidate who has done the standard independence test will feel that part (c) has settled the matter.

Part (d) then asks for the probability of both events given that at least one occurs, which is $\frac{0.25}{0.8}=\frac{5}{16}=0.3125$. The lever is that the conditioning event is now the union, not a single event, so the earlier independence verdict gives no shortcut: a candidate who reasons that dependent events must reduce the conditional probability, or who tries to reuse $\frac{5}{9}$ or $\frac{5}{12}$, will not obtain the answer. The correct route is to apply the definition of conditional probability to the event $H\cup G$.

The common error is to treat at least one as though it were a single named event and to condition on $H$ or on $G$ instead, which produces $\frac{5}{9}$ or $\frac{5}{12}$ and answers a different question. A second error is to assume that dependence forces the conditional probability of both to be smaller than $0.25$, whereas it is in fact larger. The numbers $0.6$, $0.45$ and $0.25$ were chosen so that the union is exactly $0.8$ and the required fraction reduces to $\frac{5}{16}$, a value distinct from both conditional probabilities computed earlier.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 4.6 bullet on combined events, mutually exclusive events, conditional probability and independence. The lever is that the conditioning event in the final part is the union H or G rather than a single event, so the independence verdict reached in part (c) cannot be reused to shortcut part (d). The probabilities P(H) = 0.6, P(G) = 0.45 and P(H and G) = 0.25 were chosen so that the union is exactly 0.8, so that the two conditional probabilities reduce to the exact fractions 5/9 and 5/12, and so that the product 0.27 differs from 0.25 by just enough to make the dependence unambiguous while the union-conditioned probability 0.25/0.8 = 5/16 is distinct from both.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently in Python: the addition rule for the union, both conditional probabilities as exact fractions, the product of the marginal probabilities compared with the joint probability to decide dependence, and the union-conditioned probability as a quotient.

questions.title: The smallest number of trials that pushes a probability past 0.99
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 4.8 (binomial distribution; mean and variance of the binomial distribution)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The complement rule for at least one event turns a sum over nine terms into a single power, and the required trial count must be solved as an inequality rather than read from the distribution.
questions.question: A trial has probability of success $p=0.3$ and is repeated $8$ times, with the trials independent of one another. A calculator is required throughout.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly $3$ of the $8$ trials succeed, giving your answer correct to six decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that at least one of the $8$ trials succeeds.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the smallest number of trials for which the probability of at least one success exceeds $0.99$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the mean and the standard deviation of the number of successes in $8$ trials.

questions.answer:
**(a)** If $X$ denotes the number of successes then $X\sim B(8,0.3)$ **(M1)**. The number of ways of choosing which three trials succeed is $\binom{8}{3}=56$ **(A1)**, so $P(X=3)=56(0.3)^{3}(0.7)^{5}$ **(M1)** $=0.254122$ correct to six decimal places **(A1)**. The coefficient counts the orders in which the three successes can appear, while the two powers record the probabilities of the successes and of the failures.

**(b)** The complement of at least one success is that no trial succeeds **(M1)**, and $P(X=0)=(0.7)^{8}$ **(A1)**. Therefore $P(X\ge 1)=1-(0.7)^{8}$ **(A1)** $=0.942352$ **(A1)**. The complement rule replaces a sum of nine separate binomial terms by a single power, and it is correct because the events $X=0$ and $X\ge 1$ together exhaust the sample space.

**(c)** For $n$ trials the probability of at least one success is $1-(0.7)^{n}$ **(M1)**, and this must exceed $0.99$, so $(0.7)^{n}<0.01$ **(A1)**. Taking logarithms gives $n>\frac{\ln 0.01}{\ln 0.7}=12.91\ldots$ **(M1)**, hence the smallest whole number of trials is $n=13$ **(A1)**. The inequality reverses direction because $\ln 0.7$ is negative, and the value must be rounded up rather than to the nearest integer, since the inequality is strict.

**(d)** For a binomial distribution the mean is $np=8\times 0.3$ **(M1)** $=2.4$ **(A1)**, and the variance is $np(1-p)=8\times 0.3\times 0.7=1.68$ **(M1)**. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, so $\sqrt{1.68}=1.296148$ **(A1)**. The mean is an expected count of successes while the standard deviation is measured in the same units as that count, so the two answers are consistent with each other and both describe the same binomial count.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for identifying the binomial model with $n=8$ and $p=0.3$. The (A1) is for the coefficient $56$, and a candidate who writes $\binom{8}{3}$ without evaluating it forfeits this mark. The second (M1) is for the product of the two powers, and the (A1) requires the value to six decimal places; accept $0.254122$.

(b) Award (M1) for using the complement and (A1) for the term $(0.7)^{8}$. The third (A1) is for the correct structure one minus $(0.7)^{8}$, and the final (A1) for the numerical value. A candidate who sums the terms $P(X=1)$ to $P(X=8)$ earns full credit if the total is correct.

(c) The (M1) is for the general expression one minus $(0.7)^{n}$ and the (A1) for the inequality $(0.7)^{n}<0.01$. The (M1) is for taking logarithms, and the (A1) is for $n=13$. A candidate who rounds $12.91$ up to $13$ by inspection still earns the final mark, but one who gives $12$ forfeits it because the probability there is below $0.99$.

(d) Award (M1)(A1) for the mean $2.4$, (M1) for the variance $1.68$ and (A1) for the standard deviation $1.296148$. Accept three significant figures for the standard deviation. Follow through from an incorrect $p$ is allowed.
questions.explanation:
The item is built on the complement rule and on inverting the binomial inequality. Part (a) is a direct binomial probability and rewards candidates who can form the coefficient and the two powers. Part (b) is where the lever first appears: the phrase at least one invites a sum over eight or nine terms, but the complement reduces it to the single power $(0.7)^{8}$, and a candidate who does not see this will waste time or make an arithmetic slip.

Part (c) pushes the same idea further. The condition that the probability of at least one success exceeds $0.99$ becomes the inequality $(0.7)^{n}<0.01$, and solving it requires logarithms. The critical point is that $\ln 0.7$ is negative, so the inequality reverses when the logarithms are taken; a candidate who forgets this will obtain $n<12.91$ and answer $12$. Because $0.99$ is a strict threshold, the answer must be rounded up, and $12.91$ therefore gives $n=13$, not $12$.

Part (d) returns to the standard mean and variance formulae, $np$ and $np(1-p)$, and asks for the standard deviation rather than the variance, which catches candidates who stop one step early. The numbers $p=0.3$ and $n=8$ were chosen so that $(0.7)^{8}=0.942352$ and $(0.7)^{12}=0.986159$ fall just below $0.99$ while $(0.7)^{13}=0.990311$ rises above it, so the threshold genuinely separates consecutive trial counts. A candidate who treats the question as a single calculation, rather than as a search over whole numbers, will report $12.91$ and lose the final mark, because the question asks for a count of trials rather than for a boundary value.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 4.8 bullet on the binomial distribution and its mean and variance. The lever is the complement rule for at least one success, which converts a sum over nine binomial terms into the single power 0.7^n, and the requirement to solve 1 - 0.7^n > 0.99 as an inequality in n. The values n = 8 and p = 0.3 were chosen so that the coefficient is the small integer 56, so that 0.7^8 = 0.942352 falls below 0.99 while 0.7^12 = 0.986159 remains below it and 0.7^13 = 0.990311 rises above it, making 13 the unique smallest trial count, and so that the mean 2.4 and variance 1.68 give a standard deviation of 1.296148.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently in Python: the binomial coefficient, the exact-three probability, the complement probabilities for 8, 12 and 13 trials, the logarithm threshold locating the smallest n above 0.99, and the mean and standard deviation of the binomial distribution.

questions.title: The rearranged line that is not the regression of x on y
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 4.10 (equation of the regression line of x on y; use of the regression line for prediction)
questions.subtopic: 4.10 Equation of the regression line of x on y
questions.challenge_mechanism: The two regression lines are distinct, and reversing the earlier line by algebra produces a plausible but wrong equation that shares the point of means.
questions.question: Twelve pairs of data $(x,y)$ satisfy $\sum x=84$, $\sum y=60$, $\sum x^{2}=638$, $\sum y^{2}=380$ and $\sum xy=460$. A calculator is required throughout.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that $S_{xx}=50$ and $S_{xy}=40$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the equation of the regression line of $y$ on $x$, giving it in the form $y=a+bx$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the equation of the regression line of $x$ on $y$, giving it in the form $x=c+dy$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A student rearranges the line from part (b) to make $x$ the subject and claims that this is the regression line of $x$ on $y$. Explain why the student is wrong.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The mean of $x$ is $\bar{x}=\frac{84}{12}=7$ **(M1)** and the mean of $y$ is $\bar{y}=\frac{60}{12}=5$ **(A1)**. Then $S_{xx}=638-\frac{84^{2}}{12}=638-588=50$ **(M1)(A1)** and $S_{xy}=460-\frac{84\times 60}{12}=460-420=40$ **(A1)(AG)**. These centred sums subtract the variation already accounted for by the means, so they measure spread about the mean rather than about the origin, which is why the printed values are correct.

**(b)** The gradient of the regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $b=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=\frac{40}{50}=0.8$ **(M1)(A1)**, and the intercept is $a=\bar{y}-b\bar{x}=5-0.8\times 7=-0.6$ **(M1)(A1)**. Hence $y=-0.6+0.8x$ **(A1)**. The line passes through the point of means $(7,5)$, which is what determines the intercept once the gradient is known.

**(c)** The gradient of the regression line of $x$ on $y$ uses $S_{yy}$, and $S_{yy}=380-\frac{60^{2}}{12}=80$ **(M1)(A1)**. Therefore the gradient is $d=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{yy}}=\frac{40}{80}=0.5$ **(A1)**, and the intercept is $c=\bar{x}-d\bar{y}=7-0.5\times 5=4.5$ **(M1)**, so $x=4.5+0.5y$ **(A1)**. Exchanging the roles of the two variables replaces $S_{xx}$ by $S_{yy}$ in the denominator, which is why this gradient differs from the one in part (b).

**(d)** Rearranging the line from part (b) gives $x=\frac{y+0.6}{0.8}=1.25y+0.75$ **(M1)(A1)**. This is not the regression line of $x$ on $y$, because that line minimises the squared deviations in $x$ and has gradient $\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{yy}}=0.5$ **(M1)**. The two lines coincide only when the correlation is exactly $\pm 1$, whereas here $r=\frac{40}{\sqrt{50\times 80}}=0.632$ **(A1)(R1)**. Rearranging changes the subject of the formula but not which variable is treated as the response, so the student has reversed the equation without reversing the regression.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for either mean and the (A1) for both. Award (M1) for the centred-sum formula and (A1) for $S_{xx}=50$, then (A1) for $S_{xy}=40$ and the (AG) for the printed results. A candidate who uses $638/12$ without subtracting the mean term earns the method marks only.

(b) The (M1)(A1) pair is for the gradient $\frac{40}{50}=0.8$ and the (M1)(A1) pair for the intercept $5-0.8\times 7$. The final (A1) is for the assembled equation. Accept the line written as $y=0.8x-0.6$.

(c) The (M1)(A1) is for computing $S_{yy}=80$, and the (A1) for the gradient $0.5$. The (M1) is for the intercept using the point of means and the final (A1) for the equation $x=4.5+0.5y$. A candidate who uses $S_{xx}$ as the denominator here earns no credit for the gradient, because that is precisely the error the part is testing.

(d) Award (M1)(A1) for the rearrangement to $x=1.25y+0.75$. The (M1) is for identifying the true gradient $0.5$, the (A1) for the correlation $0.632$ and the (R1) for the explanation that rearranging does not reverse the regression. Follow through from earlier parts is allowed.
questions.explanation:
The item is about the distinction between the regression line of $y$ on $x$ and the regression line of $x$ on $y$. The two lines share the point of means $(7,5)$ but have different gradients, $0.8$ and $0.5$, because the first minimises vertical deviations and the second minimises horizontal deviations. Parts (a) to (c) compute the centred sums and both lines from the summary statistics, which is routine for a candidate who knows the formulae.

Part (d) is the lever. A student rearranges $y=-0.6+0.8x$ to obtain $x=1.25y+0.75$ and claims this is the regression of $x$ on $y$. The claim is plausible because the rearranged line does pass through the point of means, but it is wrong: the correct line has gradient $0.5$, and the two lines coincide only when the correlation is exactly plus or minus one. Here $r=\frac{40}{\sqrt{50\times 80}}=0.632$, so the discrepancy is substantial. The correlation is close to zero point six three, so the two lines are not merely different in principle but visibly separated on any plot of the data.

The classic error is to believe that making $x$ the subject converts one regression into the other. Regression is defined by which variable is treated as the response, and algebra cannot change that. The numbers were chosen so that $S_{xx}=50$, $S_{yy}=80$ and $S_{xy}=40$ give the clean gradients $0.8$ and $0.5$, and so that the reciprocal $1.25$ and the correlation $0.632$ are visibly different from the correct values, making the distinction impossible to miss.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 4.10 bullet on the equation of the regression line of x on y and its use for prediction. The lever is that the regression of x on y is not obtained by rearranging the regression of y on x, even though the rearranged line passes through the same point of means. The summary statistics sum x = 84, sum y = 60, sum x^2 = 638, sum y^2 = 380 and sum xy = 460 over n = 12 pairs were chosen so that Sxx = 50, Syy = 80 and Sxy = 40, giving the clean gradients 0.8 and 0.5, the reciprocal 1.25, the intercepts -0.6 and 4.5, and the correlation 0.632, which is far enough from one that the two regression lines are visibly distinct.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently in Python: the centred sums Sxx, Syy and Sxy, the two means, both regression gradients and intercepts, the rearrangement coefficient and constant, and the correlation coefficient.

questions.title: A defective rate that is not independent of its machine
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 4.11 (formal definition and use of the probability formulae for conditional probability, independence and the addition rule)
questions.subtopic: 4.11 Formal definition and use of the formulae for conditional probability and independence
questions.challenge_mechanism: The weighted average defective rate differs from both conditional rates, and independence must be decided by comparing a conditional probability with an unconditional one rather than by inspecting the given numbers.
questions.question: Items are produced either by machine $A$, with $P(A)=0.6$, or by machine $B$, with $P(B)=0.4$. The probability that an item is defective is $0.03$ given that it came from $A$ and $0.05$ given that it came from $B$. Let $D$ denote the event that an item is defective.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find $P(D)$, the probability that a randomly chosen item is defective.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Given that an item is defective, find the probability that it came from machine $B$, giving your answer as an exact fraction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine, showing your reasoning, whether the events 'from machine $A$' and 'defective' are independent.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The machines are adjusted so that $P(D\mid A)=P(D\mid B)=0.04$. Show that after the adjustment the events 'from machine $A$' and 'defective' are independent.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The law of total probability gives $P(D)=P(A)P(D\mid A)+P(B)P(D\mid B)$ **(M1)** $=0.6\times 0.03+0.4\times 0.05$ **(A1)** $=0.018+0.020=0.038$ **(A1)(A1)**. The two machine cases are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so the overall defective rate is the weighted average of the two conditional rates, using the machine shares as weights, which is why the overall rate lies between the two conditional rates.

**(b)** Bayes' theorem gives $P(B\mid D)=\frac{P(B)P(D\mid B)}{P(D)}$ **(M1)** $=\frac{0.4\times 0.05}{0.038}$ **(A1)** $=\frac{0.020}{0.038}=\frac{20}{38}=\frac{10}{19}$ **(A1)**. The conditioning is reversed here, so the numerator is the joint probability of $B$ and $D$, which is why the answer is not simply the given rate $0.05$ but the share of the defects attributable to machine $B$. This reversal of the conditioning is the whole content of Bayes' theorem.

**(c)** The events are independent exactly when $P(D\mid A)=P(D)$ **(M1)**. Here $P(D\mid A)=0.03$ whereas $P(D)=0.038$ **(A1)**, and these values are not equal **(R1)**. Equivalently $P(A\cap D)=0.6\times 0.03=0.018$ while $P(A)P(D)=0.6\times 0.038=0.0228$ **(A1)**, so the events are not independent when judged by the product of the marginal probabilities. Comparing the conditional rate with the overall rate is decisive because the two differ even though both numbers are small and both conditional rates lie close together.

**(d)** After the adjustment the overall rate is $P(D)=0.6\times 0.04+0.4\times 0.04=0.04$ **(M1)(A1)**, while the conditional rate is $P(D\mid A)=0.04$ **(A1)**. These are equal **(R1)(AG)**. Because the conditional rate now coincides with the unconditional rate, knowing that an item came from machine $A$ gives no information about whether it is defective, so the two events are independent, and this remains true whatever the machine shares happen to be.
questions.markscheme_notes:
(a) The (M1) is for the law of total probability with both branches. The (A1) is for the substitution, and the two remaining (A1) marks are for the two products $0.018$ and $0.020$ and for their sum $0.038$. A candidate who averages the two rates without weighting them earns only the method mark.

(b) Award (M1) for Bayes' theorem and (A1) for the substitution. The (A1) requires the exact fraction $\frac{10}{19}$; a decimal such as $0.526$ does not earn it unless the fraction is also shown.

(c) The (M1) is for the independence test $P(D\mid A)=P(D)$. The (A1) is for the value $0.038$, and the (R1) for the explicit comparison with $0.03$. The final (A1) is for the alternative product test $0.018$ against $0.0228$ and the conclusion. A bare statement that the events are dependent earns at most two marks.

(d) Award (M1)(A1) for recomputing the overall rate as $0.04$, the (A1) for the conditional rate $0.04$, and the (R1)(AG) for observing that the two are equal. Follow through from an incorrect part (a) is allowed provided the equality is correctly tested.
questions.explanation:
The item contrasts a conditional defective rate with an overall defective rate, and asks whether the machine and the defect are independent. Part (a) applies the law of total probability, giving $0.038$ as the weighted average of $0.03$ and $0.05$. Part (b) reverses the conditioning with Bayes' theorem and produces the exact fraction $\frac{10}{19}$. Both parts are standard, and they supply the numbers that the later parts need.

Part (c) is the lever. The events from machine $A$ and defective are independent exactly when $P(D\mid A)$ equals $P(D)$. Here the conditional rate is $0.03$ while the overall rate is $0.038$, so the events are dependent. Candidates frequently judge independence by looking at the two given conditional rates, $0.03$ and $0.05$, and concluding from their difference that the events must be dependent; this reasoning is not the definition, and it happens to give the wrong reason even when it gives the right verdict.

Part (d) removes the difference by setting both conditional rates to $0.04$. The overall rate then also becomes $0.04$, and the conditional and unconditional probabilities coincide, so the events become independent. The numbers were chosen so that the weighted average $0.038$ differs from both conditional rates and the fraction $\frac{10}{19}$ is exact, and so that the adjusted case gives the clean equality $0.04=0.04$. A candidate who reasons from the visible gap between $0.03$ and $0.05$ may reach the right verdict for the wrong reason, and part (d) is designed to expose that shortcut by removing the gap entirely.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 4.11 bullet on the formal probability formulae for conditional probability, independence and the addition rule. The lever is that independence must be decided by comparing the conditional defective rate P(D|A) with the overall rate P(D), not by inspecting the two given conditional rates 0.03 and 0.05. The machine shares P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.4 and the rates 0.03 and 0.05 were chosen so that the weighted average is exactly 0.038, so that Bayes' theorem gives the exact fraction 10/19, and so that the alternative product test compares 0.018 with 0.0228; the adjusted rates 0.04 were chosen so that the overall rate becomes exactly 0.04 and the independence condition holds exactly.

verification.method: Every value was recomputed independently in Python: the total probability of a defect, Bayes' theorem as an exact fraction, both sides of the independence test before adjustment, and the overall and conditional rates after adjustment.

questions.title: The inverse normal value that scales with the standard deviation
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 4.12 (standardization of normal variables, z-values; inverse normal calculations)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The same standardised value is reused across two different standard deviations, so the answer scales linearly with sigma while the z-value stays fixed.
questions.question: The random variable $X$ is normally distributed with mean $150$ and standard deviation $12$. A calculator is required throughout.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that a value of $X$ chosen at random is less than $138$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that a value of $X$ lies between $144$ and $168$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the value $x$ such that $P(X<x)=0.90$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The standard deviation is later found to be $15$ rather than $12$. Determine the new value of $x$ for which $P(X<x)=0.90$ and explain how the answer changes.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Standardising gives $z=\frac{138-150}{12}$ **(M1)** $=-1$ **(A1)**, so $P(X<138)=P(Z<-1)$ **(M1)** $=0.158655$ **(A1)**. Standardising expresses the value as a number of standard deviations below the mean, after which the standard normal distribution supplies the probability directly. The value $0.158655$ is the area of the standard normal curve to the left of minus one, and a value below the mean therefore gives a negative standardised score.

**(b)** The two standardised values are $z_{1}=\frac{144-150}{12}=-0.5$ **(M1)** and $z_{2}=\frac{168-150}{12}=1.5$ **(A1)**. Hence $P(144<X<168)=P(-0.5<Z<1.5)$ **(M1)** $=0.933193-0.308539=0.624655$ **(A1)**. Subtracting the two cumulative probabilities removes the lower tail, which is correct because the required region is bounded on both sides and the lower tail must not be counted twice.

**(c)** The standard normal value satisfying $P(Z<z)=0.90$ is $z=1.281552$ **(M1)(A1)**. Reversing the standardisation gives $x=150+1.281552\times 12$ **(M1)** $=165.379$ **(A1)**. The inverse normal returns the number of standard deviations above the mean, so multiplying by the standard deviation and adding the mean returns to the original scale of the measurement.

**(d)** The required standardised value is unchanged at $1.281552$ **(M1)**, so the new value is $x=150+1.281552\times 15$ **(A1)** $=169.223$ **(A1)**. The increase is exactly $1.281552\times 3=3.845$ **(R1)**, since the answer moves by the fixed $z$-value multiplied by the change in the standard deviation. The same standardised position therefore corresponds to a larger distance from the mean when the spread is wider, so the new value of $x$ is greater than the value found in part (c). The standardised value is a property of the ninety per cent tail alone and is completely independent of the units in which $X$ is measured.

(b) Award (M1) for the first $z$-value and (A1) for both $-0.5$ and $1.5$. The (M1) is for expressing the interval probability as a difference of cumulative values and the (A1) for $0.624655$. A candidate who adds the two tail probabilities instead of subtracting earns the method mark only.

(d) The (M1) is for recognising that the $z$-value is unchanged. The (A1) is for the substitution with $15$ and the second (A1) for $169.223$. questions.explanation:
The item is about the inverse normal calculation and how its answer depends on the standard deviation. Part (a) standardises $138$ and reads a lower-tail probability, part (b) converts an interval into the difference of two cumulative probabilities, and part (c) inverts the relationship to find the value below which ninety per cent of the distribution lies, giving $z=1.281552$ and $x=165.379$.

Part (d) is the lever. The standard deviation is changed from $12$ to $15$, and the value of $x$ for the same ninety per cent point must be recomputed. The standardised value is a property of the probability alone, so it does not change; only the multiplier does. The new answer is $150+1.281552\times 15=169.223$, and the increase over the earlier answer is exactly $1.281552\times 3=3.845$.

The common error is to believe that a larger standard deviation requires a new $z$-value, or to rescale the earlier answer by the ratio of the standard deviations while forgetting that the mean stays fixed. A candidate who does this will obtain a different and incorrect value. The numbers were chosen so that $138$ is exactly one standard deviation below the mean and $144$ and $168$ are exactly half a standard deviation below and one and a half above, so that every $z$-value is exact, and so that the two answers for $x$ differ by the clean amount $1.281552\times 3$. The point of the final part is that the standardised value belongs to the probability, not to the distribution, so it survives the change untouched while every value on the original scale is stretched.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 4.12 bullet on the standardisation of normal variables and inverse normal calculations. The lever is that the standardised value for a given tail probability is fixed, so changing the standard deviation rescales the answer linearly while leaving the z-value unchanged. The mean 150 and standard deviation 12 were chosen so that 138 standardises to exactly -1, that 144 and 168 standardise to exactly -0.5 and 1.5, and that the inverse normal value 1.281552 for the ninetieth percentile gives x = 165.379; the alternative standard deviation 15 was chosen so that the same z-value gives 169.223 and the two answers differ by exactly 1.281552 times 3.
